MSCI adopts new rules that could remove MicroStrategy (Strategy) from major indexes –
Link
MSCI formally adopted rules excluding “non-operating companies” from its Global Investable Market Indexes. Prior simulations flagged Strategy (MSTR) and Metaplanet for likely removal, while SharpLink (SBET) was placed on a watchlist. The final affected list is due Nov. 11, with rules effective after the Nov. 30 close.
MSTR is a large leveraged BTC proxy for passive index funds, so forced selling could pressure the stock and weigh on broader crypto sentiment.

tweet.text:
MSCI Adopts New Index Exclusion Rules; Strategy and Metaplanet Face Potential Removal

MSCI has adopted new rules to exclude non-operating companies from its Global Investable Market Indexes. In an earlier simulation based on May 2026 data, MSCI identified Bitcoin treasury companies Strategy (MSTR) and Metaplanet (3350) as potential removals, while Ethereum treasury company SharpLink (SBET) would be placed on a watchlist. The final list of affected constituents will be published on November 11.

The new rules, effective after the November 30 close, will exclude companies that fail an operating-assets test and trigger at least four of five financial exclusion criteria. Existing constituents must fail the screening in both of their two most recent annual filing periods before removal. MSCI will also lift temporary index restrictions on companies previously identified as holding digital assets worth at least 50% of total assets, assessing them under the new methodology instead.

AI Makes Research Faster, but Is It Killing Serendipity?
> Jonah argues that AI makes research faster and better but removes the accidental discoveries that came from browsing dictionaries, libraries, and web links.
> “AI one-shots the research, the same way looking up a word online does. You don't need to search around, so you rarely stumble onto adjacent ideas.”
Source:
https://x.com/jonah_b/status/2110891773921046586

tweet.text:
AI has made my research better. But I realized today it’s also costing me something...

When I was in middle school, I asked my grandpa what a word meant. He told me to go grab the dictionary and look it up. I asked why I couldn’t just look it up online. He said that would get me the answer for sure, but I’d be missing something. When you open a dictionary, you see all the words next to the one you’re looking up, and you end up learning a few of those too. Looking it up online gets you the one word and nothing around it. No serendipity.

Zooming out, the internet era already lost some of that serendipity. It used to be that for a research project, you had to go find a book in the library. On the way to that book, you’d see books you’d never heard of. And while you were looking through its table of contents for the information you needed, you’d inevitably pick up other concepts too.

Internet research is much more directed. What you’re trading is access to more information, faster, but
